at savne.explanation: "At savne" means to miss someone or something that is not here, like a friend, family or home. It is also used for something that is gone: "Jeg savner mine nøgler" can mean you cannot find your keys. Do not use it for missing a bus or train; for that Danes say "at misse" or "at komme for sent til".

sentence.en: I miss my family.

at se.explanation: "At se" means to see, and it covers looking at things like films and TV: "Jeg ser en film". It also means to understand, as in "Jeg kan se" (I see). "Vi ses!" is a very common goodbye meaning See you!. Do not mix it up with "at kigge", which is more about looking in a direction.

sentence.en: I can't see you.

at se på.explanation: "At se på" means to look at something, and the small word "på" is part of it. "Jeg ser på billedet" means "I am looking at the picture". It is different from "at lede efter" (to look for) and from "at se" on its own (to see). The past form is "så på" and the "have" form is "set på".

sentence.en: I am looking at the picture.

at se tv.explanation: "At se tv" means to watch TV. Danes use "se" (see) for watching. You can say "at se fjernsyn" as well, which is a bit more formal and old-fashioned. "Tv" is pronounced like the two letters "te-ve".

sentence.en: I watch TV in the evening.

at sende.explanation: "At sende" means to send, for example a letter, a parcel, a message or an email. "Jeg sender dig en besked" means "I will send you a message". The past form "sendte" and the "have" form "sendt" just add a t. A related word for a parcel is "en pakke".

sentence.da: Jeg **sender** dig en besked i aften.
sentence.en: I will send you a message tonight.

at sende en sms.explanation: "At sende en sms" means to send a text message. Literally it is "to send a text". The word "sende" changes its ending in the past: "jeg sendte" and "jeg har sendt". To say who gets it, put the person after "sende": "jeg sender dig en sms" (I send you a text).

sentence.da: Jeg **sender** dig **en sms**, når jeg er hjemme.
sentence.en: I will text you when I am home.

at servere.explanation: "At servere" means to serve food or drinks, for example in a restaurant or at home for guests. It looks like the English word, but the stress is on the middle part, "ser-VE-re". You can say "Maden bliver serveret kl. 18" (The food is served at 6 pm).

sentence.en: We serve dinner at six o'clock.

at sidde.explanation: "At sidde" means to sit, in the sense of being in a seated position: "Jeg sidder på en stol" (I am sitting on a chair). To sit down is "at sætte sig". People also "sidder" at a desk or at the computer for a long time. The past form is "sad", and the "have done" form is "siddet".

sentence.en: He is sitting on the sofa.

at sige.explanation: "At sige" means to say or to tell: "Hvad siger du?" (What are you saying?). It is used when you pass on words, so you say something to someone. A useful phrase is "Hvad betyder det?" for what does it mean, but for saying hello to someone Danish uses "at sige hej". To tell a story, use "at fortælle".

sentence.en: What are you saying?

at sige farvel.explanation: "At sige farvel" means to say goodbye. You say "Farvel" when you leave, and it can sound a little final, as if you won't meet again soon. Among friends many Danes say "hej hej" or "vi ses" (see you) instead. Use "farvel" with people you are polite to, like shopkeepers.

sentence.en: I say goodbye to my friend.

at sige goddag.explanation: "At sige goddag" means to say hello, literally "to say good day". "Goddag" is a polite, slightly old-fashioned greeting that you might use with older people or in formal settings. With friends you would normally just say "hej". The opposite is "at sige farvel".

sentence.en: I say hello to the neighbor.

at skifte tøj.explanation: "At skifte tøj" means to change your clothes, for example after sport or before going out. "At skifte" means to change or switch something. For example you can "skifte" a shirt, a bus or a job. It is a good phrase for daily routines.

sentence.da: Jeg **skifter tøj**, før vi går ud.
sentence.en: I am changing clothes before we go out.

at skrive.explanation: "At skrive" means to write: "Jeg skriver et brev" (I am writing a letter). It also covers typing and texting, so you can "skrive en besked". A writer is "en forfatter", while "en skribent" is someone who writes for a paper.

sentence.da: Jeg **skriver** en besked til min ven.
sentence.en: I am writing a message to my friend.

at skulle.explanation: "At skulle" means must, should, or to be supposed to, and it is also the usual way to say what is going to happen: "Jeg skal i skole" (I am going to school). It is followed straight by another action word, with no "at". It is more about a plan or a duty than about wanting, which is "at ville".

sentence.en: I have to work tomorrow.

at slappe af.explanation: "At slappe af" means to relax or to take it easy. The little word "af" always goes at the end. People often say "Slap af!" to mean 'Calm down' or 'Take it easy'. A relaxing evening is "en afslappet aften".

sentence.en: I relax on the sofa.

at slukke.explanation: "At slukke" means to turn something off, mostly a light, a fire or a device like a TV. "Slukke lyset" means to turn off the light. It is the opposite of "at tænde" (to turn on). For a phone or computer you can also say "at slukke for", as in "slukke for telefonen".

sentence.da: Husk at **slukke** lyset, når du går.
sentence.en: Remember to turn off the light when you leave.

at slukke for.explanation: "At slukke for" means to turn off something like the TV, the radio, the water or the heating. The word "for" stays with it. For a light you say "at slukke lyset" with no "for". The opposite is "at tænde for". Do not mix it up with "slukke" in "slukke en brand" (put out a fire).

sentence.en: Remember to turn off the water.

at slutte.explanation: "At slutte" means to end or to finish: "Filmen slutter klokken ti" (The film ends at ten). With "med" it means to stop doing something: "Jeg slutter med at ryge". A handy greeting at the end of an email is "Med venlig hilsen", which is not related. The end itself is "en slutning" or "slutningen".

sentence.en: School finishes at three o'clock.

at smage.explanation: "At smage" means to taste, both to try food and to have a certain flavour. "Det smager godt" means "It tastes good" and "Det smager af citron" means "It tastes of lemon". The word for the thing itself is "en smag" (a taste).

sentence.en: The food tastes really good.

at smile.explanation: "At smile" means to smile, just like in English. "Hun smilede til mig" means "She smiled at me". You smile at someone with "smile til". The smile itself is "et smil". A smile helps a lot when you are learning a language.

sentence.en: She smiles at me every morning.

at snakke.explanation: "At snakke" means to talk or to chat, and it is the everyday word Danes use for speaking. "Kan vi snakke sammen?" means "Can we talk?". "At tale" is a bit more formal. You can say "Jeg snakker lidt dansk" (I speak a little Danish), which is useful for learners.

sentence.en: I speak a little Danish.

at snakke om.explanation: "At snakke om" means to talk about something, and it is the casual everyday version of "at tale om". Danes say it all the time with friends. The little word "om" stays right after it, like 'about' in English.

sentence.en: We are talking about food.

at sne.explanation: "At sne" means to snow. It is used with "det" (it): "det sner" is "it is snowing". One form covers both "it snows" and "it is snowing". The word for snow itself is "sne" too, as in "Der er sne", so the context shows which one you mean.

sentence.en: It snows in Denmark in the winter.

at sove.explanation: "At sove" means to sleep: "Jeg sover godt" (I sleep well). It describes the state of sleeping, not the moment of going to bed, which is "at gå i seng". The word "at sove over" means to stay the night. A friendly goodnight is "Sov godt" (Sleep well).

sentence.en: The children are sleeping now.

at spille.explanation: "At spille" means to play a game, a sport or an instrument, or to play music: "Jeg spiller guitar" (I play the guitar) and "Vi spiller fodbold". It is also used for acting a part in a film. For children's play and for fun, Danish uses "at lege". A game is "et spil".

sentence.en: I play football with my friends.

at spille fodbold.explanation: "At spille fodbold" means to play soccer (football). The verb "spille" is used for most games and sports, and also for playing music or a role. The word "fodbold" is used without "en" here, because you play the sport in general.

sentence.en: The children play soccer every Tuesday.

at spise.explanation: "At spise" means to eat and is used for any meal: "Vi spiser aftensmad" (We eat dinner). A useful phrase is "Velbekomme", which is what you say to someone who has just eaten, a bit like Enjoy your meal. For drinking, use "at drikke".

sentence.en: We eat dinner at six o'clock.

at spørge.explanation: "At spørge" means to ask a question. You ask someone about something: "Jeg spørger ham om vejen" (I ask him about the way). Do not mix it up with "at bede", which means to ask for something or request it. The past form "spurgte" and the "have" form "spurgt" change the vowel.

sentence.en: I want to ask the teacher for help.

at spørge om.explanation: "At spørge om" means to ask about or to ask for something. You use it like "spørge om vej" (ask for directions) or "spørge om hjælp" (ask for help). To ask a plain question, "at spørge" alone is enough: "Må jeg spørge dig om noget?".

sentence.en: I ask for directions.

at spørge om vej.explanation: "At spørge om vej" means to ask someone how to get somewhere. Notice that Danish says "om vej" (about way) and does not put "the" or "a" in front. A useful question is "Undskyld, kan du fortælle mig vej til banegården?". The past form "spurgte" is spelled a little differently from the base word.

sentence.en: I asked for directions to the railway station.

at starte.explanation: "At starte" means to start, and it is used for both people and things: "Bilen starter ikke" (The car won't start) and "Vi starter i morgen". It is a bit more casual than "at begynde". It is used for engines, computers and businesses too.

sentence.en: We start on Monday.

at stave.explanation: "At stave" means to spell. You will use it a lot when you give your name: "Kan du stave det?" means "Can you spell that?". The spelling itself is "stavning". Danes often spell out names letter by letter in phone calls, so it is good to know the Danish alphabet.

sentence.en: Can you spell your name?

at stille uret.explanation: "At stille uret" is the phrase for setting a clock or watch, and you hear it most often twice a year when the clocks change. "Stille" here means to put or set, and "uret" is "the clock" (en ur is not used, it is "et ur"). You say whether it goes forward or back: "stille uret en time frem" (forward an hour) or "tilbage" (back).

sentence.da: I weekenden skal vi **stille uret** en time tilbage.
sentence.en: This weekend we have to set the clock back an hour.

at stoppe.explanation: "At stoppe" means to stop, either because something ends or because you make it end: "Bussen stopper her" (The bus stops here). You can also stop doing something with "at": "Jeg stopper med at ryge" (I am quitting smoking). A bus stop is "et stoppested". The short, sharp command is "Stop!".

sentence.en: The bus stops at the station.

at studere.explanation: "At studere" means to study, especially at a university or in a serious way: "Jeg studerer historie" (I study history). A student is "en studerende" or "en student". For learning something at home, like for a test, Danes often say "at læse til en eksamen". Note that the word ends in -ere, so the past form is "studerede".

sentence.en: She studies medicine in Aarhus.

at stå.explanation: "At stå" means to stand, but Danish uses it more broadly: things that stand upright (a bottle on a table) "står". It is also used for what is written: "Der står noget på skiltet" (Something is written on the sign). "At stå op" means to get up out of bed.

sentence.en: The car is standing in front of the house.

at stå i kø.explanation: "At stå i kø" means to stand in line or queue. "Vi står i kø til biografen" means "We are standing in line for the cinema". The word "kø" is an en-word: "en kø" (a queue). Danes are quite orderly in queues, and many shops use number tickets, so you take a number and wait.

sentence.en: We are standing in line for the cinema.

at stå op.explanation: "At stå op" means to get up out of bed in the morning, and it is literally "to stand up". It is an irregular verb: "stod" is the past form. In the perfect it uses "er" (I am), not "har": "Jeg er stået op". It is not used for standing up from a chair, where Danes say "at rejse sig".

sentence.en: I get up at seven o'clock.

at stå på ski.explanation: "At stå på ski" means to ski. In Danish you literally say that you "stand on skis". The same pattern is used for water skiing: "at stå på vandski". You say "ski" without "en" or "et" in this phrase.

sentence.da: Vi **står på ski** i Norge hver vinter.
sentence.en: We ski in Norway every winter.

at svare.explanation: "At svare" means to answer or reply. You answer a person with "svare nogen" or answer a question with "svare på et spørgsmål". "Svar!" is the quick command and "et svar" is the answer itself. It is the natural partner of "at spørge" (to ask).

sentence.en: She answers all my messages.

at svømme.explanation: "At svømme" means to swim: "Jeg svømmer i havet" (I swim in the sea). You can say "at gå til svømning" for taking swimming classes, and "at bade" for going for a swim or bath for fun. A swimming pool is "en svømmehal".

related.en: to bathe / go for a swim

sentence.en: The children are swimming in the pool.

at synes.explanation: "At synes" means to think in the sense of having an opinion: "Jeg synes, det er godt" (I think it is good). Use it for tastes and views, while "at tro" is for guesses about facts. In the past, the form "syntes" looks just like the one for the "have done" form. "Hvad synes du?" is a very useful question.

sentence.da: Jeg **synes**, det er en god ide.
sentence.en: I think it is a good idea.

at synge.explanation: "At synge" means to sing. The past form "sang" and the "have" form "sunget" change the vowel. The song itself is "en sang", and "en sanger" is a male singer. Danes love singing together, and "fællessang" (singing together) is a popular tradition.

sentence.en: She sings a beautiful song.

at sælge.explanation: "At sælge" means to sell. It is the opposite of "at købe" (to buy). The past form "solgte" and the "have" form "solgt" change the vowel. You will see "Til salg" on signs, which means "for sale".

sentence.en: They sell fresh bread in the shop.

at sætte.explanation: "At sætte" means to put or to place something so that it sits or stands, like a cup on a table. "Jeg sætter koppen på bordet" means "I put the cup on the table". Be careful not to mix it up with "at sidde" (to sit), which describes where you are. "Sæt dig" means "Sit down".

sentence.en: I put the cup on the table.

at sætte sig.explanation: "At sætte sig" means to sit down: the movement of taking a seat. Notice the little word "sig" always stays with it, and it changes to "mig" when you talk about yourself ("jeg sætter mig"). To describe already sitting, use "at sidde" instead.

sentence.en: I sit down at the table.

en salat.explanation: "En salat" can mean a mixed salad as a dish or the lettuce leaves themselves, so the context tells you which one is meant. In a restaurant you will often see it as a side dish, for example "en grøn salat" (a green salad). You say "salaten" for "the salad".

sentence.da: Jeg vil gerne have en **salat** til frokost.
sentence.en: I would like a salad for lunch.

en sandal.explanation: "En sandal" is one sandal, an open shoe for warm weather. You will mostly use the plural "sandaler", since you wear a pair. It is almost the same as the English word. "Sandalen" means the sandal.

sentence.da: Min ene **sandal** er gået i stykker.
sentence.en: One of my sandals has broken.

en sandwich.explanation: "En sandwich" is a sandwich. It usually means bread with filling that is eaten with your hands, often from a cafe. A traditional Danish lunch is instead "smørrebrød", which is open with no top slice of bread.

sentence.da: Jeg tager en **sandwich** med på arbejde.
sentence.en: I take a sandwich to work.

en seng.explanation: "En seng" means a bed. In Danish, 'the bed' is "sengen" and the plural is "senge". Useful phrases are "at gå i seng" (to go to bed) and "at stå ud af sengen" (to get out of bed). Notice that Danish says "i seng" with no word for 'the' or 'a' in the first phrase.

sentence.en: I go to bed at ten o'clock.

en serviet.explanation: "En serviet" is a napkin. You get one with your meal in a restaurant, and Danes often put one on their lap at a nice dinner. The plural doubles the "t": "servietter". It is pronounced "ser-vi-ET".

sentence.en: Do you have a napkin for me?

en side.explanation: "En side" can be a page in a book, a side of something, or a web page. The plural is "sider". "På side ti" means on page ten, and "på den anden side" means on the other side. "På den ene side.. På den anden side" is the Danish "on the one hand.. On the other".

sentence.en: Open the book on page ten.

en skadestue.explanation: "En skadestue" is an emergency room, where you go for injuries and sudden problems. Made from "skade" (injury) and "stue" (room). You go "på skadestuen" (to the ER), using "på", not "til".

sentence.da: Vi kørte på **skadestuen**, fordi han faldt.
sentence.en: We drove to the ER because he fell.

en ske.explanation: "En ske" is a spoon. You use it for soup, yoghurt and porridge. The plural is "skeer", which looks odd, but it is the right form. "En teske" and "en spiseske" are a teaspoon and a tablespoon.

sentence.en: I eat the soup with a spoon.

en skinke.explanation: "En skinke" is ham, the cured pork you put on bread or eat with a meal. In daily talk people often say "skinke" for slices of ham, as in "et stykke skinke" (a piece of ham). It is very common on Danish open sandwiches and in toasties.

sentence.da: Jeg vil have brød med **skinke** og ost.
sentence.en: I want bread with ham and cheese.

en skive.explanation: "En skive" is a slice, for example a slice of bread, cheese or sausage. You say "en skive brød" (a slice of bread) and "to skiver ost" (two slices of cheese). A slice of cake is more often "et stykke kage".

sentence.en: I want a slice of bread.

en skjorte.explanation: "En skjorte" is a shirt with a collar and buttons. A casual shirt without a collar is "en t-shirt" or "en trøje" in Danish. Note the "j" in the spelling: it is "skjorte", pronounced roughly like "skyor-te".

sentence.en: He is wearing a white shirt.

en sko.explanation: "En sko" is one shoe. The plural is the same as the single word, "sko", so "to sko" means two shoes. Add "en" for "the shoe" ("skoen") and "ene" for "the shoes" ("skoene"). Danes often take their shoes off when they come into someone's home.

sentence.da: Jeg har et hul i min **sko**.
sentence.en: I have a hole in my shoe.

en skobutik.explanation: "En skobutik" is a shoe store, from "sko" (shoes) and "en butik" (a shop). Danish likes to join words like this, so you can often guess a new word. "Skobutikken" means the shoe store. It is a good word to use when you ask for directions.

sentence.da: Jeg skal i **skobutikken** efter nye sko.
sentence.en: I am going to the shoe store for new shoes.

en skole.explanation: En skole is a school. Notice the small trick: to say that someone attends school, Danes say "i skole" with no "en" or "the", as in "Børnene er i skole". To talk about the building you say "skolen" (the school). And the word is also used in compounds like "en folkeskole", the Danish state school.

sentence.en: My daughter goes to school.

en skov.explanation: "En skov" means a forest or woods. In Danish, 'the forest' is "skoven" and the plural is "skove". Danes love a walk in the woods, called "en skovtur". Don't mix it up with "et træ" (a tree).

sentence.en: We take a walk in the forest.

en skulder.explanation: "En skulder" is a shoulder. And the word for more than one drops the e: "skuldre". It is often used with pain: "Jeg har ondt i skulderen" (My shoulder hurts). It also shows up in "at trække på skuldrene" (to shrug).

sentence.en: My shoulder hurts.

en sky.explanation: En sky is a cloud. In Danish, "the cloud" is "skyen", and more than one is "skyer". The same spelling also exists as a different word, "sky", which means shy ("Han er sky" means "He is shy"), so look at the whole sentence. "Skyet" means cloudy.

sentence.da: Der er en stor mørk **sky** over os.
sentence.en: There is a big dark cloud over us.

en skål.explanation: "En skål" is a bowl. The same word, "Skål!", is also what you say as a toast, like "Cheers!". Be careful: the toast is said without "en", while the bowl is "en skål" with an article. The plural "skåle" is used for several bowls.

sentence.en: I eat soup from a bowl.

en smartphone.explanation: "En smartphone" is a phone that can run apps and use the internet, just like in English. Danes often just say "en mobil" instead, which covers any mobile phone. You say "en smartphone" and "min smartphone".

sentence.en: My smartphone is almost new.

en smerte.explanation: "En smerte" is a pain. It is mostly used in the more than one form: "Jeg har smerter" means "I am in pain". For a pain in one place, Danes often say "ondt", as in "Jeg har ondt i hovedet". "Smerte" sounds a bit more formal or serious.

sentence.en: I have pain in my back.

en sms.explanation: "En sms" is a text message sent from a phone, said "es-em-es". The plural has an apostrophe: "sms'er". Danes also use it as a verb: "at sms'e" or "at sende en sms". For messages in chat apps, "en besked" is more usual.

sentence.da: Jeg sender dig en **sms** i aften.
sentence.en: I will send you a text message tonight.

en snack.explanation: "En snack" is a small bite to eat between meals, borrowed from English, and it means the same thing. It can be something healthy like fruit or something like chips. In the plural the word is just "snacks". For a small thing to eat you can also say "en bid mad".

sentence.da: Jeg tager en **snack** med i skole.
sentence.en: I take a snack to school.

en sodavand.explanation: "En sodavand" is a fizzy soft drink, such as cola or lemonade. It is built from "soda" and "vand" (water). You can ask for "en cola" or "en appelsinsodavand" for a specific kind, and for more than one you say "to sodavand".

sentence.en: May I have a soda, please?

en sofa.explanation: "Sofa" is a sofa or couch. Danes say "i sofaen" for on the sofa, because you sit in it. It is the main seat of a living room, so you will meet it together with "en stue" (a living room) and "et bord" (a table).

sentence.en: The cat sleeps on the sofa.

en sok.explanation: "En sok" is a sock. Like with shoes, you mostly say the plural "sokker", since socks come in pairs. A pair is "et par sokker". "En strømpe" is the more general word for sock or stocking. If one goes missing, say "Jeg mangler en sok" (I am missing a sock).

sentence.en: I am missing a sock.

en sol.explanation: En sol is a sun. In daily life you almost always hear it as "solen" (the sun), as in "Solen skinner" (the sun is shining). You say "i solen" for "in the sun", for example when you sit outside. It is also found in many words about the weather and holidays, such as "solskin" (sunshine) and "en solbrille" (sunglasses).

sentence.en: The sun is shining today.

en sommer.explanation: En sommer is a summer. And "the summer" is "sommeren". The more-than-one form is shorter than you might guess: "somre". Useful phrases are "om sommeren" (in the summer, in general) and "i sommer" (this summer). Danish summers are short but bright, with long evenings.

sentence.en: It is warm in the summer.

en sommerferie.explanation: "En sommerferie" is a summer vacation or summer holiday. It is made from "sommer" (summer) and "ferie" (holiday). Many Danes take several weeks off in July, so you will often hear "i sommerferien" (during the summer vacation).

sentence.en: We are going to Spain in the summer vacation.

en sovs.explanation: "En sovs" is a sauce or gravy. It is the brown gravy you get with roast pork or meatballs in traditional Danish food. Another everyday spelling you may see is "sauce", but "sovs" is the usual Danish form.

sentence.en: The meatballs taste good with brown gravy.

en spisning.explanation: "Spisning" is a meal as an event, usually an organised one where people sit down together, as in a club or a community dinner. For the plain food you eat on an ordinary day, Danes use "et måltid" or just "mad". You will often see it in "fællesspisning", a shared community dinner that is popular in Denmark.

sentence.da: Der er en fælles **spisning** i aften.
sentence.en: There is a shared dinner tonight.

en station.explanation: En station is a station, a place where trains, metros or buses stop. You say "på stationen" for "at the station". In Danish, "the station" is "stationen". If you want to be clear that it is for trains, you can say "en togstation". It is stressed on the last part, "sta-SHOHN".

sentence.da: Toget kommer til **stationen** om fem minutter.
sentence.en: The train comes to the station in five minutes.

en stegepande.explanation: "En stegepande" is a frying pan. It is built from "stege" (to fry) and "pande" (pan), written as one word. You cook with it on the stove. Many Danes also say just "en pande". The ending "-pande" is the same as in "en pande" (a pan), so you can guess related words like "en wokpande".

sentence.en: I fry eggs in the frying pan.

en sten.explanation: "Sten" means a stone or a rock you can pick up. "Stones" looks exactly like "a stone" ("sten"), and only "the stones" ("stenene") shows it is more than one. As a material it has no article: "et hus af sten" is "a house of stone".

sentence.en: There is a stone on the road.

en stjerne.explanation: En stjerne is a star, either in the sky or as a rating, for example a hotel with "fem stjerner" (five stars). In Danish, "the star" is "stjernen". The "stj" at the start is said a bit like "st-y", and the j is hardly heard. On a clear night you can see many stars.

sentence.da: Vi kan se mange **stjerner** i nat.
sentence.en: We can see many stars tonight.

en stol.explanation: "En stol" means a chair. In Danish, 'the chair' is "stolen" and the plural is "stole". It goes naturally with the verb "at sidde": "at sidde på en stol" (to sit on a chair). A soft armchair is "en lænestol".

sentence.en: Sit on the chair.

en storebror.explanation: "En storebror" is an older brother, literally "big brother". Danes use it for any brother who is older than you, whatever the gap. The younger one is "en lillebror". In the plural the vowel changes: "storebrødre".

sentence.en: My big brother lives in Copenhagen.

en storesøster.explanation: "En storesøster" is an older sister, literally "big sister". It is used for any sister who is older than you. The younger one is "en lillesøster". The plural drops an e: "storesøstre".

sentence.da: Min **storesøster** er tre år ældre end mig.
sentence.en: My big sister is three years older than me.

en storm.explanation: "Storm" is a proper storm with strong wind, and Danes use it for the autumn and winter storms that sweep in from the North Sea. The plural is "storme" (not "stormer"), which is easy to get wrong. A gentler wind is just "blæst", and a hurricane is "en orkan".

sentence.en: A storm is coming tonight.

en strand.explanation: En strand is a beach, the sandy or stony edge of the sea. Danes love their beaches in summer. Note that you say "på stranden" (literally "on the beach") where English says "at the beach" or "on the beach". And "the beach" is "stranden".

sentence.en: We are going for a walk on the beach.

en strømpe.explanation: "En strømpe" is a stocking or a sock. In everyday talk, many Danes say "en sok" for a short sock, and "strømpe" is used for longer ones or in a general way. You will also see "strømpebukser" (tights). The plural is "strømper".

sentence.da: Jeg har et hul i min **strømpe**.
sentence.en: I have a hole in my sock.

en stue.explanation: "En stue" is a living room, the room where you sit, relax and have guests. It also gives names to floors: "stuen" or "stueetagen" is the ground floor. Some people also say "opholdsstue" for it, but "stue" is the normal word.

sentence.da: Vi sidder i **stuen** og ser tv.
sentence.en: We sit in the living room and watch TV.

en størrelse.explanation: "En størrelse" means a size, for clothes, shoes or anything else. In a shop you can ask "Hvilken størrelse har du?" (What size are you?) or "Har I den i en større størrelse?" (Do you have it in a bigger size?). It comes from "stor" (big). Clothing sizes are often just letters like S, M and L.

sentence.da: Har I den i en anden **størrelse**?
sentence.en: Do you have it in another size?

en støvle.explanation: "En støvle" is one boot. Most often you hear the plural "støvler", because boots come in pairs. They are made for cold or wet weather, and "gummistøvler" are rubber boots for rain. The word "the" goes on the end: "støvlen".

sentence.en: My left boot is wet.

en suppe.explanation: "En suppe" is a soup. Soups are popular in the cold Danish months, for example "tomatsuppe" or "hønsekødssuppe" (chicken soup). You eat soup with a spoon, "en ske", and the verb is "at spise" (to eat), not "at drikke".

sentence.da: Jeg vil gerne have **suppen** som forret.
sentence.en: I would like the soup as a starter.

en sweater.explanation: "En sweater" is a sweater, borrowed from English. In Danish, "en sweater" is a bit more modern than "en trøje", but both words are widely understood. The word for more than one is "sweatere".

sentence.en: I am wearing a grey sweater.

en sygdom.explanation: "En sygdom" is a disease or illness. It comes from "syg" (sick). To say you are sick, use "jeg er syg", and for the thing you have, use "en sygdom". Be careful with "smerte", which is pain, not illness.

sentence.en: He has a serious illness.

en sygeplejerske.explanation: "En sygeplejerske" is a nurse. It is a long word, but it breaks into "syge" (ill), "pleje" (care) and "-rske" (a female worker). Many men work as nurses too, and they are also called "sygeplejerske" in Danish, so it is not only used for women.

sentence.da: Min søster er **sygeplejerske** på et hospital.
sentence.en: My sister is a nurse at a hospital.

en sø.explanation: En sø is a lake, a body of fresh water with land all around it. Denmark has lots of them, especially in Jutland, so you will hear the word often when people talk about walks and swimming. In Danish, "the lake" is "søen". Do not mix it up with "et hav" (the sea), which is much bigger and salty.

sentence.en: We swim in the lake in the summer.

en søn.explanation: "En søn" is a son. Note the "ø", a letter that does not exist in English. It sounds a bit like the vowel in "bird". The word for a daughter is "en datter", and "et barnebarn" is a grandchild.

sentence.en: My son goes to school.

en søster.explanation: "En søster" is a sister. The plural is "søstre", with the "e" of the ending dropped. You can say "storesøster" for a big sister and "lillesøster" for a little sister. The word "søskende" covers brothers and sisters together.

sentence.en: My sister is a teacher.

et sekund.explanation: Et sekund is a second, the shortest normal unit of time. In Danish, "the second" is "sekundet". Note that "second" in the sense of "number two" is a different word ("anden" or "andet"). In everyday speech "et øjeblik" (a moment) is a very common way to say that something will only take a short while.

sentence.en: It only takes a second.

et skab.explanation: "Et skab" means a cupboard, a cabinet or a closet, any closed storage space. In Danish, 'the cupboard' is "skabet". A kitchen cupboard, a clothes closet and a locker are all "et skab", with another word added to be exact.

sentence.en: The plates are in the cupboard.

et skib.explanation: Et skib is a ship, a large boat that sails on the sea. For a small boat Danes use "en båd", and for a ferry "en færge". In Danish, "the ship" is "skibet". Denmark has a long history of sailing and shipping, so the word is used a lot, also in compound words like "et krydstogtskib" (a cruise ship).

sentence.en: The ship sails to Norway tonight.

et skæg.explanation: "Et skæg" is a beard. And it looks the same when you talk about more than one. "En mand med skæg" means a man with a beard. A moustache is "et overskæg", and "at barbere sig" means to shave.

sentence.en: My father has a long beard.

et soveværelse.explanation: "Et soveværelse" is a bedroom. It is built from "sove" (to sleep) and "værelse" (room), so it is a sleeping room. When people describe a home they often say how many they have: "en lejlighed med to soveværelser".

sentence.en: Our apartment has two bedrooms.

et spejl.explanation: "Et spejl" is a mirror. You find one in the bathroom or hall. The word looks hard to say, so practise: "spejl" sounds a little like "spile". You look "i spejlet" (in the mirror).

sentence.da: Der er et stort **spejl** i badeværelset.
sentence.en: There is a big mirror in the bathroom.

et spil.explanation: "Et spil" is a game, like a board game, card game or computer game. The plural is the same as the single form: "spil". It comes from the verb "at spille" (to play).

sentence.en: Shall we play a game?

et sprog.explanation: "Et sprog" is a language. The plural is the same as the singular: "tre sprog" is three languages. Useful questions are "Hvilket sprog taler du?" (Which language do you speak?) and "Taler du engelsk?". The verb for speaking is "at tale" or "at snakke".

sentence.en: Danish is a difficult language.

et spørgsmål.explanation: "Et spørgsmål" is a question. The plural is the same as the singular, so "to spørgsmål" means two questions. The verb "at spørge" means to ask. A polite way to start is "Må jeg stille et spørgsmål?" (May I ask a question?), literally "put a question".

sentence.en: I have a question.

et sted.explanation: "Et sted" is a place or a spot. It combines nicely: "et sted" (somewhere), "alle steder" (everywhere), "ingen steder" (nowhere). The plural is "steder". For a spot where you sit or stand, "en plads" is also common.

sentence.da: Er der et **sted** at spise her?
sentence.en: Is there a place to eat here?

et stoppested.explanation: "Et stoppested" is a place where a bus or other transport stops to let people on and off. It is built from "stoppe" (stop) and "sted" (place). For a bus you can also say "et busstoppested". Look for the next one on the display inside the bus.

sentence.en: The next stop is the railway station.

et stykke.explanation: "Et stykke" is a piece or a slice of something, such as cake or bread. The plural is "stykker". In shops it also means "each", so "ti kroner stykket" means ten kroner each. "Et stykke kage" is a piece of cake.

sentence.en: May I have a piece of cake?

et supermarked.explanation: "Et supermarked" is a supermarket, a big shop with food and everyday goods. "the" goes on the end: "supermarkedet". Common Danish chains include Netto, Føtex and Rema 1000. Many Danes just say "Jeg skal i Netto" (I am going to Netto).

sentence.en: I am going to the supermarket for milk.

et svar.explanation: "Et svar" is an answer. The plural is the same as the singular. The verb is "at svare", to answer, as in "Svar mig!". "Tak for svaret" means thanks for the reply. It is the natural partner of "et spørgsmål".

sentence.en: I know the answer.

et svin.explanation: "Et svin" is a pig, the animal. The word for more than one stays the same: "to svin". Be careful: calling a person "et svin" is an insult, a bit like "swine". For the meat, Danes say "svinekød" (pork).

sentence.en: The farmer has a pig on the farm.

et sygehus.explanation: Et sygehus is a hospital. It is built from "syg" (sick) and "hus" (house). You say "på sygehuset" for "at the hospital". Danes also say "et hospital" and use both words, so you will hear both. In Danish, "the hospital" is "sygehuset".

sentence.en: He is at the hospital.

et sår.explanation: "Et sår" is a wound or a sore, such as a cut or a scrape. And it looks the same with more than one. You put a plaster on it: "et plaster". A small cut can also be called "et lille sår".

sentence.en: I have a wound on my knee.

salt.explanation: "Salt" is salt, and it is an et-word, so "the salt" is "saltet". It is not counted, so you say "noget salt" for some. The same word also describes taste: "det er for salt" means "it is too salty". At the table you might ask "kan du give mig saltet?".

sentence.en: Can you give me the salt?

saltet.explanation: "Saltet" means salted, and it comes from the verb "at salte" (to salt). It stays "saltet" with both en-words and et-words, and only changes to "saltede" when there is more than one. Do not confuse it with "salt", which as an adjective means salty in taste.

sentence.en: I like eating salted fish.

samme.explanation: "Samme" means same, and it never changes its ending. It is almost always used after "den", "det" or "de" (the): "den samme" for en-words, "det samme" for et-words and "de samme" for more than one. "Det samme" is also a handy reply meaning "the same to you".

sentence.en: We have the same car.

sammen.explanation: "Sammen" means "together". It goes after the verb: "Vi spiser sammen" (We eat together). "Alle sammen" is a very common phrase meaning "everyone together", as in "Hej alle sammen!". The opposite is "alene" (alone) or "hver for sig" (each on their own).

sentence.en: We live together.

sandaler.explanation: "Sandaler" means sandals, the plural of "en sandal". Danes mostly wear them in the short summer, on the beach or on warm days. Like most plural words for clothes, you use it when you mean a pair. Add "ne" on the end to say "the sandals": "sandalerne".

sentence.en: I use sandals on the beach.

seks.explanation: Means "six". It is spelled like English "sex" in sound, but with "seks". It is the base of "seksten" (sixteen) and "tres" (sixty) is a different word. It looks the same before en-words and et-words.

sentence.en: I get up at six o'clock.

seksten.explanation: Means "sixteen". It is "seks" (six) plus "-ten". The first "s" and the "k" make a clear sound. Do not mix it up with "tres" (sixty) which sounds different. The word is the same before en-words and et-words.

sentence.en: My daughter is sixteen years old.

selv.explanation: "Selv" has two main jobs. After a person or thing it means "myself", "yourself" or "herself", as in "Jeg gør det selv" (I do it myself). At the start it means "even", as in "Selv min mor ved det" (Even my mother knows it). The meaning is usually clear from where it stands. Don't mix it up with "sig selv", which means "himself" or "themselves".

sentence.en: I make the food myself.

forms.en: Yes, and thanks to you too.

selv tak.explanation: "Selv tak" is the standard reply when someone says "tak" to you, and it means "you're welcome". It literally means "thanks yourself". It can also be used to return thanks, as in "Tak for i aftes" - "Selv tak" (Thanks for last night - Thanks to you too). Another way of saying it is "det var så lidt" (it was nothing).

sentence.en: "Thanks for the help!" - "You're welcome!"

selvfølgelig.explanation: "Selvfølgelig" means "of course" and shows that something is obvious or that you are happy to agree, as in "Må jeg låne din pen?" - "Selvfølgelig!" (May I borrow your pen? - Of course!). It is a long word, so take it one piece at a time: selv-følge-lig. It is also used as a polite way to accept a request. For "of course not", say "selvfølgelig ikke".

sentence.en: Of course you can borrow it.

senere.explanation: "Senere" means later, and it can be used about time ("Vi ses senere", See you later) and as a comparison, "later than". You can add "på dagen" or "i dag" to be clear, for example "senere i dag" (later today). Be careful: "sent" means late, as in "Det er sent" (It is late), while "senere" is the version meaning later.

sentence.en: I will call you later.

sennep.explanation: "Sennep" is mustard, and it is an en-word. Notice that the "p" is doubled when you add "the": "senneppen". It is not counted, so you say "noget sennep". Danes put it on hot dogs, which are called "pølser", and on pork.

sentence.en: I want mustard on the sausage.

sent.explanation: "Sent" means late, as in not early: "Vi kom sent hjem" (We came home late). Do not confuse it with "senere", which means later. When you want to say you are late for something, you say "Jeg er forsinket" or "Jeg kommer for sent". The opposite is "tidligt" (early).

sentence.da: Det er for **sent** at ringe nu.
sentence.en: It is too late to call now.

september.explanation: "September" is September, written with a small letter. You say "i september" for in September. The spelling is the same as in English, apart from the small letter. The month names from September to December all end in -ber, which is a handy pattern to remember.

sentence.en: It gets cooler in September.

forms.en: Will we see each other tomorrow?

ses i morgen.explanation: A friendly way to say goodbye when you know you will meet the person again tomorrow. It is short for "vi ses i morgen", which literally means "we are seen tomorrow". It works with friends, classmates and colleagues. You can swap "i morgen" for another time, like "ses i aften" (see you tonight).

sentence.en: See you tomorrow, and sleep well!

shampoo.explanation: "Shampoo" is shampoo, and it is an en-word. It is the same as in English, with the Danish spelling "shampoo". It is not counted, so you say "noget shampoo". Hotels often have it in the bathroom as "gratis shampoo".

sentence.en: Do you have shampoo for me?

shorts.explanation: "Shorts" is the same word as in English, used for short trousers. In Danish it is always plural and nothing is added to it: you say "mine shorts". The Danish word for trousers is "bukser", and you could say "korte bukser" (short trousers) too. People wear shorts in the warm summer months.

sentence.da: Det er varmt, så jeg tager **shorts** på.
sentence.en: It is warm, so I am putting on shorts.

siden.explanation: "Siden" means since, and it also gives "ago" in "for to år siden" (two years ago). A tip: Danish says "Jeg har boet her siden 2020", with "har", where English says "I have lived". It can also mean "later" at the start of a sentence.

sentence.en: I have lived here since 2020.

sidst.explanation: "Sidst" means last, in order, or at the end. It can also be about time: "sidst på dagen" is late in the day. For something that is the last one of its kind, you say "sidste" ("sidste gang", the last time). The opposite is "først" (first).

sentence.en: He came last to the party.

sidste.explanation: "Sidste" means last, both in the sense of final ("den sidste bus") and most recent ("sidste uge" is last week, "sidste år" is last year). It never changes its ending. The opposite is "første" (first), and "næste" is the word for next.

sentence.da: Det er den **sidste** bus i dag.
sentence.en: It is the last bus today.

forms.en: She is looking forward to it.

sig.explanation: "Sig" is used when the person doing something is also the one it happens to, for he, she, it and they. It means "himself", "herself", "itself" or "themselves". Many Danish verbs always come with it, such as "at glæde sig" (to look forward) and "at skynde sig" (to hurry). For I and you the words are "mig" and "dig" instead.

sentence.en: He washes himself every morning.

sikker.explanation: "Sikker" means sure or safe. "Er du sikker?" means "Are you sure?" and "Jeg er sikker" means "I am sure". For safe things it fits a place, a car or a plan. Watch the spelling: "et sikkert sted" with "t", and "sikre steder" where the "e" before the "r" disappears. The opposite is "usikker" (unsure or unsafe).

sentence.en: Are you sure about that?

sin.explanation: "Sin" means "his own", "her own" or "its own", and goes with en-words. It points back to the person doing the action: "Han ser sin bror" means he sees his own brother. "Han ser hans bror" would mean someone else's brother. It is not used for "I" or "you"; there you say "min" and "din".

sentence.en: She loves her (own) dog.

sine.explanation: "Sine" means "his own", "her own" or "their own" when you talk about more than one thing, like "sine venner". It points back to the person doing the action. It is the same for en-words and et-words. For one thing use "sin" or "sit".

sentence.en: She calls her (own) parents.

sit.explanation: "Sit" means "his own", "her own" or "its own", and goes with et-words, like "sit hus" or "sit barn". It points back to the person doing the action. For en-words use "sin", and for many things "sine". If you mean someone else's thing, use "hans" or "hendes".

sentence.en: He looks after his (own) child.

sjette.explanation: "Sjette" means sixth. It comes from "seks" (six), but the spelling changes, so watch out. It is used for the order of things and for dates: "den sjette maj" is the sixth of May. In writing you can use "6." with a dot.

sentence.en: She lives on the sixth floor.

sjov.explanation: "Sjov" means fun or funny. It covers both: a joke can be "sjov" and so can a party. "Det var sjovt" means "That was fun". It is also used on its own to mean fun: "for sjov" means "for fun" or "as a joke". Add "t" for et-words ("et sjovt spil") and "-e" for more than one. The opposite is "kedelig" (boring).

sentence.en: That was a fun evening.

skandinavien.explanation: "Skandinavien" is capitalised because it is a place name, but the adjective "skandinavisk" and the nationality words are not. In everyday Danish people often say "Norden" (the Nordic countries) when they also mean Finland and Iceland. Strictly, Scandinavia means Denmark, Norway and Sweden.

sentence.en: Denmark is in Scandinavia.

sko.explanation: "Sko" is the word for shoes, and it is almost always used in the plural. The word looks the same for one shoe and many, so you can tell by the "en" in front ("en sko" is one shoe) or by the context. Add "ene" to get "skoene" (the shoes). You say "tage skoene på" to put your shoes on.

sentence.en: I have bought new shoes.

skyet.explanation: "Skyet" means cloudy, with clouds in the sky. It comes from "en sky" (a cloud). It stays the same for en-words and et-words, but gets an "-e" when you talk about more than one thing. The opposite is "solrig". Weather forecasts also use "overskyet" for a sky fully covered by clouds.

sentence.en: It is cloudy today.

forms.da: Skynd dig, vi er sent på den.

skynd dig.explanation: "Skynd dig" means "hurry up" and is said to one person. If you speak to more than one person, say "skynd jer". The words "dig" and "jer" are small words meaning "yourself" and "yourselves". It can sound a bit pushy, so soften it with "tak" or a smile.

sentence.da: **Skynd dig**, toget går om fem minutter!
sentence.en: Hurry up, the train leaves in five minutes!

skål.explanation: "Skål" is what you say as a toast when you raise your glass, like "Cheers". Danes often look the other person in the eye when they say it. It is the same word as "en skål" (a bowl), but as a toast it is used on its own.

sentence.en: Cheers, and happy birthday!

slidt.explanation: "Slidt" means worn, and it comes from the verb "at slide" (to wear out, to toil): something worn from use. It stays "slidt" with both en-words and et-words, and becomes "slidte" when there is more than one. It is also used about people: "Jeg er helt slidt" means "I'm completely worn out".

sentence.en: The sofa is very worn.

slik.explanation: "Slik" is candy or sweets, and it is an et-word, so "the candy" is "slikket". It is normally used for sweets in general, without "et": "Jeg spiser for meget slik". Many Danish children get "lørdagsslik" (Saturday candy) as a weekly treat.

sentence.en: Children love candy.

slut.explanation: "Slut" means over or finished, and it is used after "er": "Ferien er slut" (The holiday is over). It can also mean that something has run out, as in "Mælken er slut". "Til slut" means "in the end" or "finally".

sentence.en: The school day is over.

smal.explanation: "Smal" means narrow, for streets, paths, doors, windows or even a thin face. It is the opposite of "bred" (wide). Add "t" for et-words ("et smalt hus") and "-e" when you talk about more than one thing or when "the" is in front ("de smalle gader"). It is about width, not about being thin like paper; for that use "tynd".

sentence.da: Der er en **smal** sti ned til stranden.
sentence.en: There is a narrow path down to the beach.

smuk.explanation: "Smuk" means beautiful, for people, places, views and things. It is a little stronger than "pæn" (nice-looking). Add "t" for et-words ("et smukt hus") and "-ke" for more than one: "smukke" with a double "k". The opposite is "grim" (ugly). To compliment someone's day you can say "Hvor er det smukt!" (How beautiful it is!).

sentence.da: Det er en **smuk** dag i dag.
sentence.en: It is a beautiful day today.

smør.explanation: "Smør" means butter. It is an et-word, so "the butter" is "smørret", with a doubled r. It is also the word for putting butter on something, "at smøre". Danes say "smør på brødet" for butter on the bread, and "smørrebrød" literally means bread with butter.

sentence.da: Vil du have **smør** på dit brød?
sentence.en: Do you want butter on your bread?

snart.explanation: "Snart" means soon, and with a clock time it also means almost, as in "Klokken er snart ti". The phrase "så snart" means "as soon as" and starts a part of a sentence. For "in a little while" you can also say "om lidt".

sentence.en: The food will be ready soon.

snavset.explanation: "Snavset" means dirty. It does not change with et-words ("et snavset glas"), but with more than one it becomes "snavsede" ("snavsede sko"). It comes from "snavs", which means dirt. The opposite is "ren" (clean).

sentence.en: Your shoes are very dirty.

sne.explanation: Sne is snow. It is an en-word, so "the snow" is "sneen". To say that it is snowing, you use the verb: "Det sner". Danes do not get much snow every winter, so when it falls it is a big event for children. It is also in "en snemand" (a snowman) and "en snebold" (a snowball).

sentence.en: The children are playing in the snow.

sokker.explanation: "Sokker" means socks. One sock is "en sok", and more than one is "sokker". The usual way to count them is by pairs: "et par sokker". The word "sokkerne" means "the socks". Wool socks in winter are "uldsokker".

sentence.en: My socks are wet.

solbriller.explanation: "Solbriller" means sunglasses, from "sol" (sun) and "briller" (glasses). It is always plural in Danish, and "et par solbriller" means a pair. You say "solbrillerne" for the sunglasses. The plain word for glasses you see with is "briller".

sentence.en: I have forgotten my sunglasses.

solcreme.explanation: "Solcreme" is sunscreen, the cream you put on your skin to protect it from the sun. It is built from "sol" (sun) and "creme" (cream), and it is an en-word, so "the sunscreen" is "solcremen". It is normally used without "a" when you speak in general: "Husk solcreme!".

sentence.da: Husk at tage **solcreme** med på stranden.
sentence.en: Remember to bring sunscreen to the beach.

solrig.explanation: "Solrig" means sunny. It describes a day, a place or the weather. With en-words you use "solrig", with et-words "solrigt", and with more than one "solrige". The opposite is "skyet" or "overskyet". The stronger forms are "solrigere" (sunnier) and "solrigest" (sunniest).

sentence.da: I dag er det en **solrig** dag.
sentence.en: Today is a sunny day.

solrigt.explanation: "Solrigt" is the form of "solrig" (sunny) used with et-words and when you describe the weather with "det": "Det er solrigt". Since "vejr" (weather) is an et-word, you say "solrigt vejr". It is the opposite of "skyet" or "overskyet".

sentence.en: It is sunny at the beach.

solskin.explanation: "Solskin" means sunshine, the light and warmth from the sun. It is an et-word, so "the sunshine" is "solskinnet". It is made from "sol" (sun) and "skin" (shine). A weather forecast might say "solskin og sol hele dagen", or just "der er solskin".

sentence.en: We are enjoying the sunshine in the garden.

solskinsvejr.explanation: "Solskinsvejr" means sunny weather, built from "solskin" (sunshine) and "vejr" (weather). It is an et-word. It is the opposite of "regnvejr" and "gråvejr", and Danes often use it in plans: "Hvis det er solskinsvejr, tager vi på stranden."

sentence.da: Det er dejligt at gå tur i **solskinsvejr**.
sentence.en: It is lovely to go for a walk in sunny weather.

som.explanation: "Som" is a small word with several jobs. It can mean "that", "who" or "which" and joins a describing part to a person or thing, as in "manden, som bor her" (the man who lives here). It also means "like" or "as", as in "Jeg arbejder som lærer" (I work as a teacher). When in doubt, "som" can nearly always be used for "who", "which" and "that".

sentence.da: Det er den bog, **som** jeg læser.
sentence.en: That is the book that I am reading.

somme tider.explanation: "Somme tider" means sometimes, and it is just the two-word way of writing "sommetider". Both are correct and mean the same. It is used for things that happen now and then, not always. "Nogle gange" is another everyday way to say it.

sentence.da: Jeg er **somme tider** træt om morgenen.
sentence.en: I am sometimes tired in the morning.

forms.en: I sometimes go for a walk

sommetider.explanation: "Sommetider" means sometimes, and it is used for things that happen now and then but not always. You can also write it as two words, "somme tider", with the same meaning. "Nogle gange" is another everyday way to say it.

sentence.en: Sometimes I take the bike.

sort.explanation: "Sort" means black. Unlike most colour words, it does not get a "t" with et-words: "et sort hus". When there is more than one, it adds an "e": "sorte biler". The opposite is "hvid" (white).

sentence.en: She has a black bag.

sov godt.explanation: Said to wish someone a good sleep, most often at bedtime. "Sov" is the command form of "at sove" (to sleep), and "godt" means well. It is often paired with "godnat" (good night). You can add "drøm sødt" for "sweet dreams".

sentence.en: Good night, sleep well!

spaghetti.explanation: "Spaghetti" is spaghetti, and in Danish it is an en-word, so "the spaghetti" is "spaghettien". It is not counted, so you say "noget spaghetti". A very common family dinner is "spaghetti med kødsovs" (spaghetti with meat sauce).

sentence.en: We eat spaghetti with meat sauce.

spanien.explanation: "Spanien" is Spain. Place names like this are written with a capital letter and used without "the": "i Spanien" means "in Spain" and "til Spanien" means "to Spain". A person is "en spanier" and the language is "spansk". Many Danes go there on holiday for the sun.

sentence.en: We are on holiday in Spain.

spansk.explanation: "Spansk" means Spanish, both for things from Spain and for the language. Danish does not use a capital letter for it. Before an et-word it stays "spansk" (no extra t), and before more than one thing it becomes "spanske". For the language you can say "jeg taler spansk".

sentence.en: I am learning Spanish tonight.

spinat.explanation: "Spinat" is spinach, and it is an en-word. It is not counted, so you say "noget spinat" for some spinach. You can eat it raw in a salad ("rå spinat") or cooked, for example in a lasagne or soup. The frozen kind is "frossen spinat".

sentence.en: There is spinach in the soup.

sport.explanation: "Sport" is the general word for sport, and it is an en-word. It usually has no "en" in front when you talk about sport in general: "Jeg kan lide sport". To talk about a specific sport you can say "en sportsgren", and "at dyrke sport" means to do sports.

sentence.da: Jeg ser **sport** i fjernsynet hver weekend.
sentence.en: I watch sport on TV every weekend.

spændende.explanation: "Spændende" means exciting or interesting, and it never changes its ending. It is a very handy word: "Det lyder spændende" means "That sounds exciting". It comes from "spænding" (excitement). Do not mix it up with "interessant", which is milder.

sentence.en: It is an exciting film.

stadig.explanation: "Stadig" means "still", meaning something is continuing: "Han sover stadig" (He is still sleeping). It usually comes right after the verb. A similar word "endnu" can mean "yet" or "still", but "stadig" is the safe one for ongoing things. It can also mean "steady" for a thing.

sentence.en: He is still sleeping.

stadigvæk.explanation: "Stadigvæk" means still, as in "it keeps on being so". You will also hear the shorter "stadig" with the same meaning, and it is just as common. Do not mix it up with "endnu", which is used in questions and with "ikke": "ikke endnu" (not yet).

sentence.en: He is still sleeping.

stegt.explanation: "Stegt" means fried or roasted, depending on the food. It comes from the verb "at stege", and "stegte" is used before plural words. It is used for fish, eggs, potatoes and meat that is cooked in a pan or oven. "Stegt flæsk" (fried pork) is often called Denmark's national dish.

sentence.en: I would like fried fish.

stille.explanation: "Stille" means quiet, silent or still. It does not change for en-words, et-words or more than one. "Vær stille" means "Be quiet". It is also a verb, "at stille" (to put or place, to ask a question: "at stille et spørgsmål"), which is a different use. For a quiet and calm person you can also use "rolig".

sentence.en: She is very quiet in class.

stop.explanation: The same as in English, and used the same way as a quick order to halt. "Stop" is also the base of the Danish word "at stoppe" (to stop): "bussen stopper her". On a sign it also means "stop". Add "lige" to soften it: "stop lige" is "hold on a moment".

sentence.en: Stop! I forgot my bag.

stor.explanation: "Stor" means big or large. It changes with the word it describes: nothing extra for an en-word, "-t" for an et-word (stort), and "-e" for many things or after "the" (store). It can also mean tall for a person. The opposite is "lille" (small), and "større" means bigger.

sentence.en: It is a big house.

storbritannien.explanation: "Storbritannien" is Great Britain. Place names like this are written with a capital letter and used without "the": "i Storbritannien" means "in Great Britain" and "til Storbritannien" means "to Great Britain". It is a long word made from "stor" (big) and "Britannien". People are "briter" and the describing word is "britisk". It covers England, Scotland and Wales.

sentence.en: He comes from Great Britain.

stærk.explanation: "Stærk" means strong, for people, coffee, tea, drinks, wind, spices and feelings. For a strong cup of coffee you say "stærk kaffe", and for strong cheese or chilli, "stærk" also means hot or spicy. Add "t" for et-words ("et stærkt hold") and "-e" for more than one. The opposite is "svag" (weak).

sentence.en: He is very strong.

størst.explanation: "Størst" means biggest or largest. It is the top step after "stor" (big) and "større" (bigger). Alone it stays "størst" ("Han er størst"), but before a word it adds an "e": "den største". Note that the "-st" sound ends the word, like English "-est".

sentence.da: København er den **største** by i Danmark.
sentence.en: Copenhagen is the biggest city in Denmark.

støvler.explanation: "Støvler" means boots, the plural of "en støvle". Danes wear them a lot in the wet and cold months, and rubber boots are called "gummistøvler". When you want to say the boots, the word "the" goes on the end: "støvlerne". It is a good word for the clothes and shopping topics.

sentence.da: Det regner, så jeg tager **støvler** på.
sentence.en: It is raining, so I am putting boots on.

sukker.explanation: "Sukker" is sugar, an et-word, so "the sugar" is "sukkeret". Like in English it is usually used without "et": "lidt sukker" (a little sugar). Danes often ask "Vil du have sukker i kaffen?" (Do you want sugar in your coffee?).

sentence.en: Do you want sugar in your coffee?

sulten.explanation: "Sulten" means hungry. You say "Jeg er sulten" (I am hungry) just like in English. Add "t" for et-words ("et sultent barn") and the "e" drops out for more than one: "sultne". The word for hunger is "sult" (hunger). The opposite is "mæt" (full after eating). Do not use "sulten" for something you want in a general way; it only means being hungry for food.

sentence.en: I am really hungry.

sund.explanation: "Sund" means healthy, for food, habits or a person. It adds a "t" with et-words ("sundt") and an "e" for more than one ("sunde"). Do not confuse it with "rask", which means well or not sick right now. "Sund" is how good something is for you in general.

sentence.en: Fruit is healthy.

sundhed.explanation: "Sundhed" is health in a general sense, such as public health or how healthy a lifestyle is. It has no plural and no "en" or "et" in front. For your own personal health, for example when you ask how someone is doing physically, Danes usually say "helbred" instead.

sentence.en: Health is more important than money.

super.explanation: "Super" means super or great, and it never changes its ending. Danes use it a lot, alone as "Super!" or before another word to make it stronger: "super god" is really good. It is casual and friendly, so it fits everyday talk.

sentence.en: That is a great idea!

svensk.explanation: "Svensk" is written with a small letter, and the plural is "svenske". A Swedish person is "en svensker", and the language is also "svensk". Written Swedish and Danish are close, but spoken Swedish can be hard for Danes to follow at first.

sentence.en: My neighbour is Swedish.

sverige.explanation: "Sverige" is Sweden. Place names like this are written with a capital letter and used without "the": "i Sverige" means "in Sweden" and "til Sverige" means "to Sweden". The people are "svenskere" (one person is "en svensker"), and the language is "svensk". It lies just across the water from Denmark, over the Øresund bridge.

sentence.en: We are driving to Sweden at the weekend.

svimmel.explanation: "Svimmel" means dizzy, the feeling that the room is spinning. It adds a "t" with et-words ("svimmelt"), and for more than one it becomes "svimle" and drops one m. You often say "Jeg er svimmel" or "Jeg bliver svimmel" (I get dizzy).

sentence.da: Jeg er **svimmel**, fordi jeg ikke har spist.
sentence.en: I am dizzy because I have not eaten.

svinekød.explanation: "Svinekød" is pork. It is built from "svin" (pig) and "kød" (meat), and it is an et-word. Pork is very common in Danish cooking, for example in "frikadeller" (meatballs) and "flæskesteg" (roast pork).

sentence.en: Danes eat a lot of pork.

svær.explanation: "Svær" means difficult or hard to do. Add "t" for et-words ("et svært ord") and "-e" for more than one. It can also mean big or heavy in older or fixed phrases, but as a beginner you will mostly need the meaning difficult. Its opposites are "let" and "nem" (easy). Danes often say "Det er svært" when something is hard to do.

sentence.da: Danske ord kan være **svære** at sige.
sentence.en: Danish words can be difficult to say.

svømning.explanation: "Svømning" is swimming as a sport or activity. It is an en-word and usually has no "en" in front. The verb is "at svømme" (to swim). A typical phrase is "Jeg går til svømning", which means you have regular swimming lessons or training.

sentence.en: The children go to swimming on Mondays.

syd.explanation: "Syd" means south, one of the four main directions. It is used in compound words such as "Sydjylland" (southern Jutland) and "sydpå" (towards the south). It is the opposite of "nord". Warm holiday places are often said to be "i syd" or "sydpå".

sentence.da: Mange tager **syd** på ferie om sommeren.
sentence.en: Many people go south on holiday in the summer.

sydamerika.explanation: "Sydamerika" is South America, written as one word with a capital letter. It is made of "syd" (south) and "Amerika". Say "i Sydamerika" for being there and "til Sydamerika" for going there. The matching word for North America is "Nordamerika".

sentence.en: She has travelled around South America.

syg.explanation: "Syg" means sick or ill. "Jeg er syg" is what you say when you cannot go to work or school. To report in sick, Danes say "melde sig syg". Add "t" for et-words ("et sygt barn") and "-e" for more than one. The opposite is "rask" (healthy, recovered). "Sygdom" is the word for an illness and "en læge" is a doctor.

sentence.en: My son is sick today.

syltetøj.explanation: "Syltetøj" is jam, an et-word, so "the jam" is "syltetøjet". It is a long word, but it breaks into "sylte" (to preserve) and "tøj" (stuff). You spread it on bread, pancakes or porridge, and it is often said as "lidt syltetøj" without "et".

sentence.da: Jeg vil have **syltetøj** på mit brød.
sentence.en: I want jam on my bread.

sytten.explanation: Means "seventeen". It comes from "syv" (seven), but the "v" drops out, so it is "sytten" and not "syvten". The ending is shared with the other teens. It stays the same before en-words and et-words, for example "sytten år" (seventeen years).

sentence.en: He is seventeen years old.

syv.explanation: Means "seven". The "v" at the end is soft and sounds almost like a short "u". It stays the same before en-words and et-words. Seventeen is "sytten", where the "v" drops out, and seventy is "halvfjerds".

sentence.da: Der er **syv** dage i en uge.
sentence.en: There are seven days in a week.

syvende.explanation: "Syvende" means seventh. It comes from "syv" (seven). It is used for the order of things and for dates: "den syvende juli" is the seventh of July. In writing you can use "7." with a dot after the number.

sentence.da: Det er min **syvende** uge i Danmark.
sentence.en: It is my seventh week in Denmark.

så.explanation: "Så" means so or then. It can show a result ("Det regner, så vi bliver hjemme"), a next step ("og så går vi") or strength ("så stor"). Careful: "så" is also the past form of "at se", as in "Jeg så ham" (I saw him).

sentence.da: Først spiser vi, og **så** går vi hjem.
sentence.en: First we eat, and then we go home.

forms.en: Stay as long as you like

så længe.explanation: "Så længe" starts a part of a sentence and means "as long as". There, little words like "ikke" come before the verb ("så længe du ikke vil"), unlike in a simple sentence. On its own it can also mean "for now" or "in the meantime", as in "Det er fint så længe".

sentence.da: Du må bo her, **så længe** du vil.
sentence.en: You may live here as long as you want.

sådan.explanation: "Sådan" means "like that", "such" or "this way". "Sådan en bil" is "a car like that" and "Gør det sådan" is "Do it like this". Said on its own, "Sådan!" is like "There you go!". It is also used in "sådan set" (more or less). For et-words you will see "sådant".

sentence.en: You do it like this.

sæbe.explanation: "Sæbe" is soap, and it is an en-word. It is not counted, so you say "noget sæbe". For a single bar you can say "et stykke sæbe" (a piece of soap). Hand soap is "håndsæbe" and dish soap is "opvaskemiddel" (a different word).

sentence.en: I wash my hands with soap.

sød.explanation: "Sød" means sweet in taste ("sød kage") and also sweet or cute for people, animals and small children. Calling someone "sød" is friendly and warm. A common phrase is "Tak, det er sødt af dig" (Thank you, that is sweet of you). Add "t" for et-words ("et sødt barn") and "-e" for more than one. The opposite for taste is "sur" (sour) or "bitter".

sentence.en: How sweet she is!

sølv.explanation: "Sølv" is silver, both the metal and the color. It is an et-word, and there is no plural because it is a material. Put it in front of another word to make things: "en sølvring" is a silver ring. The color is also used for the second-place medal.

sentence.en: My ring is made of silver.

søndag.explanation: "Søndag" is Sunday, the day many families spend together, and traditionally a day when many shops are closed or open shorter hours. Say "på søndag" for the coming Sunday and "om søndagen" for every Sunday. Remember the ø, and write it with a small letter.

sentence.en: We are visiting my mother on Sunday.
